title: Scenes, Collision, and Physics in Godot

body.narration: A scene organizes an object. Collision defines its boundary and filtering. A movement policy decides what happens over time. Keep those responsibilities separate, and a missing pickup becomes a testable question instead of a mysterious physics bug.
body.motion: Build a scene hierarchy, add the boundary, then move the same actor through a sensor.
body.why: The spatial or temporal transformation is the claim; a physical-object metaphor would obscure its exact geometry.

body.narration: This lab ran in Godot four point seven point two. Match your documentation and project settings to the installed engine. A saved version is reproducible context; calling something the latest release is a claim that soon expires.
body.motion: Reveal the recorded version, then the actual project feature line.
body.why: Verbatim recorded output establishes the observation and keeps its evidence limits visible.

body.narration: A scene is a reusable node tree, usually saved as a text scene file. One root owns this small example. A complete level, a player, a coin, and a menu can each be scenes.
body.motion: Reveal the root and then its child in the actual engine-saved scene.
body.why: Exact runnable source is the teaching target; a full editor layout would reduce usable code size.

body.narration: Node itself has no position. Two D and three D spatial nodes provide transforms. Here a child keeps its local offset when its parent moves. Top-level settings and different node types can change that relationship.
body.motion: Move a parent and child together while a local-offset ruler stays fixed.
body.why: The spatial or temporal transformation is the claim; a physical-object metaphor would obscure its exact geometry.

body.narration: PackedScene holds a saved definition. Instantiate creates a live copy. These two copies have different positions, while resources inside them may still be shared. Independent nodes do not automatically mean independent materials or shapes.
body.motion: Highlight instantiate twice, then the two distinct assigned positions.
body.why: Exact runnable source is the teaching target; a full editor layout would reduce usable code size.

body.narration: A level has a player and coins: composition. An inherited scene specializes a base scene: a variant relationship. Prefer exported settings over repeatedly exposing editable children. Reuse should preserve a clear boundary around the object.

body.narration: Let the level connect a coin's collected signal to the score update. The coin reports what happened without locating a distant parent. Unique names help inside a scene; persistent state can live in an autoload.
body.motion: Trace the signal from coin to level, then a separate call from level to score.

body.narration: A question block remembers whether it was used, so give it a small scene and an explicit state. Animate its visual child for a cosmetic bump. If the solid surface must push something, use an animatable body.
body.motion: Highlight the used guard before the state change and deferred spawn.
body.why: Exact runnable source is the teaching target; a full editor layout would reduce usable code size.

body.narration: Keep actors, blocks, levels, interface, and layer definitions organized by responsibility. Test scenes in isolation. When editing text scenes, preserve resource references and existing identifiers; letting the engine save a PackedScene avoids hand-copying node identifiers.
body.motion: Reveal the engine pack-and-save calls, then their real saved artifact.
body.why: Exact runnable source is the teaching target; a full editor layout would reduce usable code size.

body.narration: A static body resists impacts. It can represent a wall or provide conveyor velocity without moving its geometry. A platform following a path belongs on an animatable body, with its movement synchronized to physics.
body.motion: Keep a conveyor outline fixed while the surface arrow moves; move the whole platform in the paired panel.
body.why: The spatial or temporal transformation is the claim; a physical-object metaphor would obscure its exact geometry.

body.narration: A rigid body asks the solver to calculate motion. Forces sustain a push; an impulse produces a one-time change. For this isolated example, mass two and impulse one hundred twenty predict a velocity change of sixty.
body.motion: Reveal mass, then the impulse call; keep the recorded measured result beside the code.
body.why: Exact runnable source is the teaching target; a full editor layout would reduce usable code size.

body.narration: A character body gives your code collision and sliding helpers. It does not supply your game's gravity or friction policy. Set velocity in pixels per second, then call move and slide once in the physics callback.
body.motion: Reveal the velocity update before the movement call.
body.why: Exact runnable source is the teaching target; a full editor layout would reduce usable code size.

body.narration: An area detects overlaps without blocking the player. It can also change local gravity or damping. Body-entered is for bodies; area-entered is for areas. Detection needs monitoring and a mask that includes the target's layer.
body.motion: Focus the actual overlapping sensor and player, then its recorded award counter.
body.why: A real captured artifact exists and directly supports the claim; reconstructed output would add no evidence.

body.narration: Artwork is not collision geometry. A rectangle gives crisp platformer edges; a capsule gives smoother rounded contacts. Resize the shape resource instead of scaling the physics node. Keep collision shapes as direct children of their body.
body.motion: Hold one silhouette while swapping rectangle and capsule boundaries; then expand shape dimensions without scaling the body.
body.why: The spatial or temporal transformation is the claim; a physical-object metaphor would obscure its exact geometry.

body.narration: Name categories before assigning bits: world, one-way platforms, player, enemy, pickup, hazard, and debris. The player scans world and platforms. The coin scans player. Debris scans world. This table makes deliberate exclusions visible.
body.motion: Build the seven-category matrix, highlighting each scan row on its spoken cue.
body.why: The spatial or temporal transformation is the claim; a physical-object metaphor would obscure its exact geometry.

body.narration: The layer-value methods take one-based layer numbers. Layer three corresponds to bit value four. A raw mask combines bits; the Inspector displays named categories. Keep one constants file synchronized with the project layer names.
body.motion: Reveal the bit conversion, then the checked value four.
body.why: Exact runnable source is the teaching target; a full editor layout would reduce usable code size.

body.narration: Our coin detected the player even though the player did not scan pickups. Removing the area's mask prevented detection. That is a directed area query. Do not turn it into a universal rule that every body pair needs reciprocal masks.
body.motion: Show the two actual mask-test records in sequence and hold the contrast.
body.why: Verbatim recorded output establishes the observation and keeps its evidence limits visible.

body.narration: Two nodes can share the same Shape resource. Resize that shared resource and both boundaries change. Duplicate the resource when you need one independent boundary. This is resource ownership, separate from whether the nodes were instanced separately.
body.motion: Highlight the shared shape assignment, then the duplicate before resize.
body.why: Exact runnable source is the teaching target; a full editor layout would reduce usable code size.

body.narration: Move and slide consumes the velocity property and applies the timestep internally. Move and collide takes a displacement, often velocity times delta. Mixing these contracts is a common source of tiny movement or wildly incorrect speed.
body.motion: Compare the two executed method forms side by side with their units.
body.why: Exact runnable source is the teaching target; a full editor layout would reduce usable code size.

body.narration: Choose jump height and time to the apex. Under constant upward-phase acceleration, gravity is twice the height divided by time squared. Initial upward speed is gravity times apex time. Godot's downward-positive axis makes jump velocity negative.
body.motion: Derive the two equations, substitute seventy-two pixels and zero point three eight seconds, and draw the rising arc.
body.why: The spatial or temporal transformation is the claim; a physical-object metaphor would obscure its exact geometry.

body.narration: The reference controller computes rise gravity from those design values. It increases gravity while falling and clamps fall speed. That creates a deliberate game feel. These parameters describe a policy, not an attempt at a universal realistic jump.
body.motion: Highlight rise gravity, falling multiplier, and terminal-speed clamp in spoken order.
body.why: Exact runnable source is the teaching target; a full editor layout would reduce usable code size.

body.narration: Horizontal speed approaches a target rather than jumping instantly. Ground acceleration, braking, and air acceleration are separate choices. Multiply acceleration by delta when updating velocity; keep the final movement call responsible for displacement.
body.motion: Highlight the rate selection, then move_toward with rate times delta.
body.why: Exact runnable source is the teaching target; a full editor layout would reduce usable code size.

body.narration: Coyote time permits a jump shortly after leaving a ledge. Jump buffering remembers a recent press before landing. They are different timer windows. Consume both when a jump starts so a held permission cannot launch another jump.
body.motion: Move a press marker across the two timing windows; clear both tokens on launch.
body.why: The spatial or temporal transformation is the claim; a physical-object metaphor would obscure its exact geometry.

body.narration: Releasing jump early reduces upward speed for a shorter hop. A stomp bounce sets a new upward velocity. If you author gravity yourself, area gravity overrides do not automatically replace that policy; decide how local gravity should contribute.
body.motion: Highlight release cut, then bounce; retain their signs and fractional multipliers.
body.why: Exact runnable source is the teaching target; a full editor layout would reduce usable code size.

body.narration: Up direction and the maximum floor angle classify surfaces. Floor snap helps follow downward slopes; grounded and floating modes serve different movement styles. Read floor state after movement for the current result, or deliberately use the previous result for coyote time.
body.motion: Focus actual floor-angle and snap properties, then movement-mode entries.
body.why: A real captured artifact exists and directly supports the claim; reconstructed output would add no evidence.

body.narration: Move an animatable platform on physics ticks and test inherited velocity when the character leaves. Characters can affect other bodies, but a deliberate crate-pushing policy may use impulses. That policy only runs when the character actually collides with the crate.
body.motion: Highlight platform physics movement; then show the explicit impulse branch and mask prerequisite.
body.why: Exact runnable source is the teaching target; a full editor layout would reduce usable code size.

body.narration: The continuous formula is a design target. A fixed-step controller samples it. Here the measured apex is slightly above seventy-two pixels, within the declared ten-percent tolerance. Plot the measured samples before changing parameters to chase a feeling.
body.motion: Reveal the actual engine trajectory against the target line and tolerance band.
body.why: The spatial or temporal transformation is the claim; a physical-object metaphor would obscure its exact geometry.

body.narration: Physics overlap callbacks can run while queries are being flushed. Defer changes such as disabling a shape or monitoring. The coin sets a synchronous claimed flag first, then schedules the physics change and emits its value.
body.motion: Highlight the guard, immediate latch, deferred monitoring, and signal in order.
body.why: Exact runnable source is the teaching target; a full editor layout would reduce usable code size.

body.narration: We invoked the collection path again after the first award. The count remained one. Deferring monitoring alone leaves a window before that change applies. A small immediate latch makes the gameplay promise explicit.
body.motion: Reveal the first successful award and repeated-call check from the actual log.
body.why: Verbatim recorded output establishes the observation and keeps its evidence limits visible.

body.narration: A falling player above an enemy can suggest a stomp, but comparing origins alone is a heuristic. Feet-aligned pivots help interpretation. A top sensor or contact-normal test, plus side and corner tests, makes the intended rule clearer.
body.motion: Contrast a top approach with a side approach at similar heights; keep the heuristic boundary visible.
body.why: The spatial or temporal transformation is the claim; a physical-object metaphor would obscure its exact geometry.

body.narration: This example uses a separate top sensor for a falling player's stomp. A side sensor requests damage. The defeated latch prevents repeated events, and sensor changes are deferred. Simultaneous corner contacts still need an explicit priority policy.
body.motion: Highlight top and side signal connections, then the defeated guard.
body.why: Exact runnable source is the teaching target; a full editor layout would reduce usable code size.

body.narration: A TileSet owns tile collision polygons and their physics categories. TileMapLayer places cells and builds the bodies. A stateful block is often easier as its own scene; repeated terrain suits tiles. Keep their responsibilities distinct.
body.motion: Reveal the TileSet physics layer and polygon before the cell placement call.
body.why: Exact runnable source is the teaching target; a full editor layout would reduce usable code size.

body.narration: This collision touched cell three, zero. The body's resource identifier mapped to quadrant zero, zero. Physics chunking groups compatible tile geometry, so the body identifier does not uniquely identify the struck cell. Disabling chunking changes that tradeoff.
body.motion: Focus the real touched tile and the two recorded coordinate results.
body.why: A real captured artifact exists and directly supports the claim; reconstructed output would add no evidence.

body.narration: Probe slightly into the hit surface, against its outward normal. Convert that world point into the tile layer's local coordinates, then map it to a cell. The probe distance is example-specific; test transformed layers and contacts near cell boundaries.
body.motion: Highlight point minus normal, coordinate conversion, and the resulting cell lookup.
body.why: Exact runnable source is the teaching target; a full editor layout would reduce usable code size.

body.narration: The checked four point seven shape reference exposes a one-way direction. The default points down in two D coordinates. This is a body collision feature, not an area's overlap policy. Test tilted platforms rather than assuming older tutorial behavior.
body.motion: Focus the actual direction property and its Area2D exclusion.

body.narration: Separate one-way surfaces onto their own layer, then temporarily stop scanning it. A short physics timer is a simple drop-through policy. Before restoring collision in a real game, ensure the character has cleared the platform and handle overlapping requests.
body.motion: Highlight the mask toggle, physics timer, and restoration limitation.
body.why: Exact runnable source is the teaching target; a full editor layout would reduce usable code size.

body.narration: Physics ticks and rendered frames are different clocks. The default physics rate is sixty ticks per second. Run collision-based motion in physics callbacks and use delta. Correctly scaled render-frame motion still does not give the same collision scheduling.
body.motion: Draw uniform physics ticks and denser render samples on separate aligned timelines.
body.why: The spatial or temporal transformation is the claim; a physical-object metaphor would obscure its exact geometry.

body.narration: Speed divided by tick rate estimates travel per tick. It is not a collision theorem. Our character's swept movement detected a four-pixel floor across a requested three-hundred-pixel displacement. Method, shape, direction, and backend all matter.
body.motion: Focus the actual thin floor and collision result after showing the requested displacement.
body.why: A real captured artifact exists and directly supports the claim; reconstructed output would add no evidence.

body.narration: For fast rigid bodies, continuous collision detection can reduce tunneling. Two D provides ray and shape modes; three D exposes its own settings. Also consider thicker collision geometry and a higher physics rate. None is a universal prevention guarantee.
body.motion: Focus the actual rigid-body continuous-detection property and available modes.
body.why: A real captured artifact exists and directly supports the claim; reconstructed output would add no evidence.

body.narration: Interpolation draws intermediate poses between physics states. It smooths presentation without simulating extra contacts. Temporarily testing at ten ticks per second makes mistakes obvious. Restore the intended rate and test pixel snapping and camera behavior together.
body.motion: Hold two physics positions and move the displayed pose between them; keep the physics markers fixed.
body.why: The spatial or temporal transformation is the claim; a physical-object metaphor would obscure its exact geometry.

body.narration: A respawn is a discontinuity. Set the new position, clear unwanted velocity, then reset physics interpolation. For a rigid body, change the simulated state through its integration callback. Frequent transform writes can fight the solver.
body.motion: Reveal position, velocity reset, and interpolation reset in sequence.
body.why: Exact runnable source is the teaching target; a full editor layout would reduce usable code size.

body.narration: A fixed timestep improves consistency, but it is not a promise of identical physics across runs, devices, or backends. Grade documented structure and behavior within tolerances. Exact replay requirements need a separate determinism design and validation plan.
body.motion: Focus the official physics discussion while distinguishing tick rate from replay guarantees.
body.why: A real captured artifact exists and directly supports the claim; reconstructed output would add no evidence.

body.narration: A missed coin suggests filtering. An offset boundary suggests scale or a shared resource. A wrong tile suggests contact lookup. A slope flicker suggests movement order or snap. Treat each as a hypothesis, then change one variable and rerun.

body.narration: The lab ran real physics checks and captured real engine output. Those records cover specific setups. They do not prove good controls, all corner contacts, cross-device stability, or moving-platform behavior. Read diagnostics as well as the process exit code.

body.narration: For this jump, ten percent means a band around the design height. A point inside the band passes this measurement; it does not validate every movement rule. Keep structural checks, numerical checks, and a human playtest as separate evidence.

body.narration: Godot's two D and three D physics are separate systems. Jolt is now built into Godot and is the default for new projects in the checked documentation. Existing projects keep their selected backend; inspect the setting before interpreting behavior.

body.narration: The same responsibilities transfer to three D nodes. Start with boxes, spheres, or capsules. Convex shapes suit movable objects; a few convex pieces can approximate a complex outline. Concave triangle collision is generally for static environments and costs more.
